description: The blue of the Olympic high meadows: a leafy perennial lupine, 25-70 cm, with hand-shaped leaves of five to eleven leaflets and dense spikes of blue-purple pea flowers. In late July whole slopes of Hurricane Ridge and the Bailey Range turn blue with it, mixed with paintbrush and aster.

season_notes.winter: Gone below ground under the snowpack.
season_notes.spring: Leaves push up through the wet ground as the snow melts in June.
season_notes.summer: Blue-purple spikes in July and August, the banner's white patch turning purple after pollination.
season_notes.fall: Hairy pods split and twist; the stalks dry tan before the first snow.

range.where: subalpine meadows and alpine ridges of the Olympic and Cascade mountains (var. subalpinus, Burke): Hurricane Ridge, Obstruction Point, Seven Lakes Basin, the Bailey Range; the species from Alaska to California

notes: Drawn from miniature lupine (same genus, the 'mound' habit with 'palmate' leaves and a blue 'spike') as a bigger perennial with a subalpine calendar: under snow November to May, up in June, flowering July-August, the stalks dried tan by October. Burke: 0.3-2.4 m for the species (the subalpine variety is the short end), 5-11 leaflets 4-10 cm long, racemes 16-60 cm, flowers blue, purple or white, June-August, var. subalpinus in the Olympics and Cascades. Burke files the Olympic plants under Lupinus latifolius var. subalpinus; some floras (and some of Burke's photo captions) use Lupinus arcticus subsp. subalpinus for the same plants, so that name is an alias; which is current needs a local botanist. Black-tailed deer graze it; Olympic marmots eat lupine heavily, and elk and mountain goats graze the meadows; only the deer is in the animal library. The forb slot limit noted on the sword fern card applies.
